records.title: Grade 5 - Integrated U.S. History
records.subject: social-studies

records.title: USHG ERA 1 – BEGINNINGS TO 1620
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Individually and collaboratively, students will engage in planned inquiries to understand how early European exploration and colonization resulted in cultural and ecological interactions among previously unconnected peoples.

records.title: Indigenous Peoples’ Lives in the Americas
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the lives of the Indigenous Peoples living in North America prior to European contact.

records.title: Use maps to locate peoples in the Eastern Woodland (the Woodland Peoples east of...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use maps to locate peoples in the Eastern Woodland (the Woodland Peoples east of the Mississippi River), desert Southwest, the Pacific Northwest, and the nomadic nations of the Great Plains.

records.title: Compare how Indigenous Peoples in the Eastern Woodland and another tribal region...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Compare how Indigenous Peoples in the Eastern Woodland and another tribal region adapted to or modified the environment.

records.title: Describe Eastern Woodland life with respect to governmental and family structures,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe Eastern Woodland life with respect to governmental and family structures, trade, and their relationship to the land.

records.title: European Exploration
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Identify the causes and consequences of European exploration and colonization.

records.title: Explain the technological and political developments that made sea exploration...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain the technological and political developments that made sea exploration possible.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the invention of the astrolabe, improved maps, the rise of nation-states.

records.title: Use case studies of individual explorers and stories of life in Europe to compare...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use case studies of individual explorers and stories of life in Europe to compare the goals, obstacles, motivations, and consequences for European exploration and colonization of the Americas.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the economic, political, cultural, and religious consequences of colonization, including who was impacted.

records.title: African Life Before the 16th Century
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the lives of peoples living in West Africa prior to the 16th century.

records.title: Use maps to locate the major regions of Africa (North Africa, West Africa, Central...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use maps to locate the major regions of Africa (North Africa, West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Southern Africa).

records.title: Describe the life and cultural development of people living in West Africa before...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the life and cultural development of people living in West Africa before the 16th century with respect to economic (the ways people made a living) and family structures, and the growth of states, towns, and trade.

records.title: Three World Interactions
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the environmental, political, and cultural consequences of the interactions among European, African, and Indigenous Peoples in the late 15th century through the 17th century.

records.title: Describe the convergence of Europeans, Indigenous Peoples, and Africans in the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the convergence of Europeans, Indigenous Peoples, and Africans in the Americas after 1492 from the perspective of these three groups.

records.title: Use primary and secondary sources to compare Europeans, Africans, and Indigenous...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use primary and secondary sources to compare Europeans, Africans, and Indigenous Peoples who converged in the Western Hemisphere after 1492 with respect to governmental structure, and views on property ownership and land use.

Examples may include but are not limited to: letters, diaries, maps, documents, narratives, pictures, graphic data.

records.title: Explain the cultural impact that occurred between the British, French, and Spanish...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the cultural impact that occurred between the British, French, and Spanish on the lives of Indigenous Peoples.

records.title: Describe the Columbian Exchange and its impact on Europeans, Indigenous Peoples,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the Columbian Exchange and its impact on Europeans, Indigenous Peoples, and Africans.

records.title: USHG ERA 2 – COLONIZATION AND SETTLEMENT (1585-1763)
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Individually and collaboratively, students will engage in planned inquiries to understand how European values and institutions transferred to and modified in the colonies, and how slavery reshaped European and African life in the Americas.

records.title: European Struggle for Control of North America
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Compare the regional settlement patterns and describe significant developments in Southern, New England, and the Mid-Atlantic colonies.

records.title: Describe significant developments in the Southern colonies, including:
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe significant developments in the Southern colonies, including:

- patterns of settlement and control, including the impact of geography (land-forms and climate) on settlement.

- the establishment of Jamestown.

- the development of one-crop economies (plantation land use and growing season for rice in Carolinas and tobacco in Virginia).

- interactions with Indigenous Peoples, including the trading of goods, services, and ideas among Europeans and Indigenous Peoples.

- the development of colonial representative assemblies (House of Burgesses).

- the development of slavery.

records.title: Describe significant developments in the New England colonies, including:
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe significant developments in the New England colonies, including:

- patterns of settlement and control including the impact of geography (land-forms and climate) on settlement.

- interactions with Indigenous Peoples, including the trading of goods, services, and ideas among Europeans and Indigenous Peoples, growth of agricultural (small farms) and non-agricultural (shipping, manufacturing) economies.

- the development of government, including the establishment of town meetings, development of colonial legislatures, and growth of royal government.

- religious tensions in Massachusetts that led to the establishment of other colonies in New England.

records.title: Describe significant developments in the Middle colonies, including:
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe significant developments in the Middle colonies, including:

- patterns of settlement and control, including the impact of geography (land-forms and climate) on settlement.

- interactions with Indigenous Peoples, including the trading of goods, services, and ideas among Europeans and Indigenous Peoples.

- the growth of economies in the Middle colonies, the Dutch settlement in New Netherlands, Quaker settlement in Pennsylvania, and subsequent English takeover of the Middle colonies.

- immigration patterns leading to ethnic diversity in the Middle colonies.

records.title: Compare the regional settlement patterns of the Southern colonies, New England,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Compare the regional settlement patterns of the Southern colonies, New England, and the Middle colonies.

records.title: Explain the economic, political, cultural, and religious causes of migration to...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the economic, political, cultural, and religious causes of migration to colonial North America.

records.title: European Slave Trade and Slavery in Colonial America
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze the development of the slave system in the Americas and its impact.

records.title: Describe Triangular Trade, including:
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe Triangular Trade, including:

- the trade routes.

- the people and goods that were traded.

- the Middle Passage.

- the impact on life in Africa.

records.title: Describe the lives of enslaved Africans and free Africans, including fugitive and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the lives of enslaved Africans and free Africans, including fugitive and escaped slaves in the American colonies.

records.title: Describe how enslaved and free Africans struggled to retain elements of their...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe how enslaved and free Africans struggled to retain elements of their diverse African histories and cultures to develop distinct African-American identities.

Examples may include but are not limited to: Gullah Islands, Louisiana, The Carolinas.

records.title: Life in Colonial America
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Distinguish among and explain the reasons for regional differences in colonial America.

records.title: Locate the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies on a map.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Locate the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies on a map.

records.title: Describe the daily lives of people living in the New England, Middle, and Southern...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the daily lives of people living in the New England, Middle, and Southern colonies.

records.title: Describe colonial life in America from the perspectives of at least three...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe colonial life in America from the perspectives of at least three different groups of people.

Examples may include but are not limited to: perspectives of wealthy landowners, farmers, merchants, indentured servants, laborers, the poor, women, enslaved people, free Africans, and Indigenous Peoples.

records.title: Describe the development of the emerging labor force in the colonies.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the development of the emerging labor force in the colonies.

Examples may include but are not limited to: cash-crop farming, slavery, indentured servants.

records.title: Make generalizations about the reasons for regional differences in colonial America.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Make generalizations about the reasons for regional differences in colonial America.

records.title: USHG ERA 3 REVOLUTION AND THE NEW NATION (1754-1800)
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Individually and collaboratively, students will engage in planned inquiries to investigate the causes of the American Revolution, the ideas and interests involved in forging the revolutionary movement, and the reasons for the American victory.

records.title: Causes of the American Revolution
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Identify the major political, economic, and ideological reasons for the American Revolution.

records.title: Describe how the French and Indian War affected British policy toward the colonies...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how the French and Indian War affected British policy toward the colonies and subsequent colonial dissatisfaction with the new policy.

records.title: Describe the causes and effects of events such as the Stamp Act, the Boston...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the causes and effects of events such as the Stamp Act, the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, and the Intolerable Acts.

records.title: Using an event from the Revolutionary era, explain how British and colonial views...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Using an event from the Revolutionary era, explain how British and colonial views on authority and the use of power without authority differed (views on representative government).

Examples may include but are not limited to: the Boston Tea Party, quartering of soldiers, writs of assistance, the closing of colonial legislatures.

records.title: Describe the role of the First and Second Continental Congresses in unifying the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the role of the First and Second Continental Congresses in unifying the colonies.

Examples may include but are not limited to: addressing the Intolerable Acts, declaring independence, drafting the Articles of Confederation.

records.title: Use the Declaration of Independence to explain why many colonists wanted to...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use the Declaration of Independence to explain why many colonists wanted to separate from Great Britain and why they believed they had the right to do so.

records.title: Identify the role that key individuals played in leading the colonists to...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Identify the role that key individuals played in leading the colonists to revolution, including George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Franklin, Patrick Henry, Samuel Adams, John Adams, and Thomas Paine.

records.title: Describe how colonial experiences with self-government and ideas about government...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe how colonial experiences with self-government and ideas about government influenced the decision to declare independence.

Examples may include but are not limited to: Mayflower Compact, House of Burgesses and town meetings; the Iroquois Confederacy; protecting individual rights and promoting the common good; natural rights; limited government; representative government.

records.title: Identify a problem that people in the colonies faced, identify alternative choices...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Identify a problem that people in the colonies faced, identify alternative choices for addressing the problem with possible consequences, and describe the course of action taken.

records.title: The American Revolution and its Consequences
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the multi-faceted nature of the American Revolution and its consequences.

records.title: Describe the advantages and disadvantages each side had during the American...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages each side had during the American Revolution with respect to military leadership, geography, types of resources, and motivations.

records.title: Describe the importance of Valley Forge, the Battle of Saratoga, and the Battle of...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the importance of Valley Forge, the Battle of Saratoga, and the Battle of Yorktown in the American Revolution.

records.title: Investigate the role of women, enslaved and freed Africans, Indigenous Peoples,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Investigate the role of women, enslaved and freed Africans, Indigenous Peoples, and France in helping shape the outcome of the war.

records.title: Describe the significance of the Treaty of Paris (establishment of the United...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the significance of the Treaty of Paris (establishment of the United States and its initial boundaries).

records.title: Creating New Government(s) and a New Constitution
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain some of the challenges faced by the new nation under the Articles of Confederation, and analyze the development of the Constitution as a new plan for governing.

records.title: Describe the powers of the national government and state governments under the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the powers of the national government and state governments under the Articles of Confederation.

records.title: Give examples of problems the country faced under the Articles of Confederation.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Give examples of problems the country faced under the Articles of Confederation.

Examples may include but are not limited to: lack of national army, competing currencies, reliance on state governments for money.

records.title: Explain why the Constitutional Convention was convened and why the Constitution...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain why the Constitutional Convention was convened and why the Constitution was written.

records.title: Describe the issues over representation and slavery the Framers faced at the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the issues over representation and slavery the Framers faced at the Constitutional Convention and how they were addressed in the Constitution.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the Great Compromise, the Three-Fifths Compromise.

records.title: Give reasons why the Framers wanted to limit the power of government.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Give reasons why the Framers wanted to limit the power of government.

Examples may include but are not limited to: fear of a strong executive, representative government, and the importance of individual rights.

records.title: Describe the principle of federalism and how it is expressed through the sharing...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the principle of federalism and how it is expressed through the sharing and distribution of power as stated in the Constitution.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the Tenth Amendment, enumerated powers, reserved powers.

records.title: Describe the concern that some people had about individual rights and why the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the concern that some people had about individual rights and why the inclusion of a Bill of Rights was needed for ratification.

records.title: Describe the rights of individuals protected in the Bill of Rights (the first 10...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the rights of individuals protected in the Bill of Rights (the first 10 amendments) to the U.S. Constitution.

records.title: Compare and contrast different ideas about the purposes of government in different...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Compare and contrast different ideas about the purposes of government in different nations, nation-states or governments.

Examples may include but are not limited to: protecting individual rights, promoting the common good, providing economic security, molding the character of citizens, or promoting a particular religion. Purposes may also include keeping an ethnic group or party in power. Governments may include those of nation-states, newly independent states, emerging states, and other governmental entities such as tribal governments.

records.title: Nature of Civic Life, Politics, and Government
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe civic life, politics, and government and explain their relationships.

records.title: PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze how people identify, organize, and accomplish the purposes of government.

records.title: Define the characteristics of modern nation-states.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Define the characteristics of modern nation-states.

Examples may include but are not limited to: a specific territory, clearly defined boundaries, citizens, collect taxes and provide services, jurisdiction over people who reside there, laws, and government.

records.title: Compare and contrast various forms of government around the world.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Compare and contrast various forms of government around the world.

Examples may include but are not limited to: democracies, parliamentary systems, dictatorships, oligarchies, and theocracies.

records.title: Characteristics of Nation-States
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the characteristics of nation-states and how they may interact.

records.title: STRUCTURE AND FUNCTIONS OF GOVERNMENT
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain that governments are structured to serve the people. Describe the major activities of government, including making and enforcing laws, providing services and benefits to individuals and groups, assigning individual and collective responsibilities, generating revenue, and providing national security.

records.title: Explain how governments address national and international issues and form...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how governments address national and international issues and form policies, and how the policies may not be consistent with those of other nation-states.

Examples may include but are not limited to: climate change, and human and civil rights; within the United States, federal/tribal relations in the United States.

records.title: Explain the challenges to governments to address global issues, and the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the challenges to governments to address global issues, and the international cooperation needed to do so.

records.title: Analyze the impact of treaties, agreements, and international organizations on...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Analyze the impact of treaties, agreements, and international organizations on global issues.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) or subsequent agreements, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the Organization of American States (OAS), the United Nations (UN), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the Paris Climate Accord.

records.title: Conflict and Cooperation Between and Among Nations
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the various ways that governments interact both positively and negatively.

records.title: RELATIONSHIP OF UNITED STATES TO OTHER GOVERNMENTS, WORLD ISSUES, AND WORLD GOVERNING ORGANIZATIONS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain ways in which governments interact with one another through trade, diplomacy, treaties and agreements, humanitarian aid, economic sanctions and incentives, military force, and the threat of force.

records.title: CIVICS AND GOVERNMENT
records.subject: social-studies

records.title: Explain how incentives and disincentives in the market economy can change the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how incentives and disincentives in the market economy can change the decision-making process.

Examples may include but are not limited to: acquiring money, profit, and goods; wanting to avoid loss of position in society; job placement; taxes on cigarettes to discourage smoking; raising prices to increase profit.

records.title: Individual, Business, and Government Choices
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how individuals, businesses, and government make economic decisions when confronting scarcity or surpluses in the market economy.

records.title: THE MARKET ECONOMY
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the market economy in terms of the relevance of limited resources, how individuals and institutions make and evaluate decisions, the role of incentives, how buyers and sellers interact to create markets, how markets allocate resources, and the economic role of government in a market economy.

records.title: Analyze the impact of sanctions, tariffs, treaties, quotas, and subsidies.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Analyze the impact of sanctions, tariffs, treaties, quotas, and subsidies.

Examples may include but are not limited to: implications of economic sanctions on all countries involved.

records.title: Role of Government
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how national governments make decisions that affect the national economy.

records.title: THE NATIONAL ECONOMY
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use economic concepts, terminology, and data to identify and describe how a national economy functions and to study the role of government as a provider of goods and services within a national economy.

records.title: Explain and compare how economic systems (traditional, command, market) answer the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain and compare how economic systems (traditional, command, market) answer the three basic economic questions: What goods and services will be produced? How will they be produced? For whom will they be produced? Also, who will receive the benefits or bears the costs of production?

records.title: Compare and contrast the economic and ecological costs and benefits of different...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Compare and contrast the economic and ecological costs and benefits of different kinds of energy production.

Examples may include but are not limited to: oil, coal, natural gas, nuclear, biomass, solar, hydroelectric, geothermal, wind, and the impact of each.

records.title: Economic Systems
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how societies organize to allocate resources to produce and distribute goods and services.

records.title: Use charts and graphs to compare imports and exports of different countries in the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use charts and graphs to compare imports and exports of different countries in the world and propose generalizations about patterns of economic interdependence.

records.title: Diagram or map the flow of materials, labor, and capital used to produce a...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Diagram or map the flow of materials, labor, and capital used to produce a consumer product.

Examples may include but are not limited to: global supply chain, computer production, automobile production.

records.title: Explain how communication innovations have affected economic interactions and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how communication innovations have affected economic interactions and where and how people work.

Examples may include but are not limited to: Internet-based home offices, international work teams, international companies, online shopping.

records.title: Economic Interdependence
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe patterns and networks of economic interdependence, including trade.

records.title: INTERNATIONAL ECONOMY
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze reasons for individuals and businesses to specialize and trade, why individuals and businesses trade across international borders, and the comparisons of the benefits and costs of specialization and the resulting trade for consumers, producers, and governments.

records.title: ECONOMICS
records.subject: social-studies

records.title: Use a variety of geographic tools (maps, globes, and web-based geography...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use a variety of geographic tools (maps, globes, and web-based geography technology) to analyze the world at global, regional, and local scales.

Examples may include but are not limited to: looking for the significance of location, making comparisons among places and regions, identifying spatial patterns and comparing patterns, exploring how places and people are connected as well as how people are part of, use, and impact the environment. Spatial analysis can also involve looking at an issue at different scales in order to provide different insights.

records.title: Draw a sketch map, or add information to an outline map, of the world or a world...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Draw a sketch map, or add information to an outline map, of the world or a world region.

Examples may include but are not limited to: locate the following on a world map: the United States, North and South America, Africa, Europe, and Asia; continents; oceans; and latitude lines — equator, Prime Meridian, tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, Arctic and Antarctic circles using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), drawing, or web-based programs.

records.title: Spatial Thinking
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use maps and other geographic tools to acquire and process information from a spatial perspective.

records.title: Apply the skills of geographic inquiry (asking geographic questions, acquiring...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Apply the skills of geographic inquiry (asking geographic questions, acquiring geographic information, organizing geographic information, analyzing geographic information, and answering geographic questions) to analyze a geographic problem or issue.

records.title: Explain why maps of the same place may vary, including the perspectives and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain why maps of the same place may vary, including the perspectives and purposes of the cartographers.

Examples may include but are not limited to: different countries may label disputed territories differently, remote sensing images provide information not visible to humans.

records.title: Use, interpret, and create maps and graphs representing population...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use, interpret, and create maps and graphs representing population characteristics, natural features, and land use of the region under study.

records.title: Use images as the basis for answering geographic questions about the human and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use images as the basis for answering geographic questions about the human and physical characteristics of places and major world regions.

Examples may include but are not limited to: pictures, aerial photos, and remote sensing images.

records.title: Locate and use information from GIS and satellite remote sensing to answer...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate and use information from GIS and satellite remote sensing to answer geographic questions.

Examples may include but are not limited to: Google Earth and ArcGIS on-line have multiple teacher applications. Clickable PDFs provide overlay strategies for students without technology skills.

records.title: Create or interpret a map of the population distribution of a region and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Create or interpret a map of the population distribution of a region and generalize about the factors influencing the distribution of the population.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how natural characteristics are associated with sparse population densities, how different combinations of natural and human factors lead to different densities, and why major cities are located where they are.

records.title: Geographical Inquiry and Analysis
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use skills of geographic inquiry and analysis to answer important questions about relationships between people, their cultures, and their environments, in their communities and within the larger world context. Students use information to make reasoned judgments based on the authenticity of the information, critically analyze the information, and present the results.

records.title: Use the fundamental themes of geography (location, place, human-environment...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use the fundamental themes of geography (location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, region) to describe regions or places on earth.

Examples may include but are not limited to:

- “place” deals with the natural and human characteristics of a place while “location” deals with where the place is, especially relative to other places.

- “human-environment interaction” deals with resources, human adaptation, and human impact, as well as natural catastrophes.

- “movement” includes migration of people, transportation of goods and services, and the diffusion of information, as well as the movement of material in natural cycles, such as water through hydrology.

- “regions” are generalizations about the common characteristics of areas.

records.title: Explain the different ways in which places are connected and how those connections...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the different ways in which places are connected and how those connections demonstrate interdependence and accessibility.

records.title: Geographical Understanding
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: The purpose of middle school geography curriculum is to develop content, themes, skills, and perspectives that can help students understand a diverse and interconnected world.

records.title: THE WORLD IN SPATIAL TERMS: GEOGRAPHICAL HABITS OF MIND
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
The use of technology has dramatically enhanced the ability of teachers and students to see the world in different ways. Geo-spatial technology includes geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing, and global positioning systems (GPS), and the ability to look at places all around the world has allowed students to do geography, not just learn it.

Learning how to use technology is only part of learning to think spatially. Geographically literate people: know about our complex interconnected world; understand science and social science concepts; use maps, data and geo-spatial technologies; and use spatial reasoning. Spatial reasoning involves the following: looking at patterns; analyzing connections between places; understanding how the conditions at one place can be similar or very different from another; trying to understand how location is important; and seeing why some characteristics tend to occur together in places.

Geographers also look at the world with an ecological perspective. What are the relationships within ecosystems, and what role do humans have in using, modifying, and adapting to different environments from a local to global scale?

records.title: Locate and describe the basic patterns of landforms.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate and describe the basic patterns of landforms.

Examples may include but are not limited to: patterns at a continental scale or larger.

records.title: Locate and describe the basic patterns and processes of plate tectonics.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate and describe the basic patterns and processes of plate tectonics.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the location of continental plates and the Ring of Fire. Processes include plate movement, uplift, earthquakes, and volcanism.

records.title: Locate and describe the characteristics and patterns of major world climates and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate and describe the characteristics and patterns of major world climates and ecosystems.

Examples may include but are not limited to: tropical wet and tropical wet-dry, arid and semi-arid, sub-tropical, continental, and arctic climates. Ecosystems include tropical rain forest, savanna, grassland, desert, temperate and coniferous forests, tundra, oceans, and ice caps.

records.title: Physical Characteristics of Places
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the physical characteristics of places.

records.title: Describe the human characteristics of the region under study, including languages,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the human characteristics of the region under study, including languages, religions, economic system, governmental system, cultural traditions.

records.title: Explain how communities are affected positively or negatively by changes in...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how communities are affected positively or negatively by changes in technology.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how changes in transportation and communication technology influence where people live, how changes in manufacturing influence where factories are located, and how changes in energy technology reduce or increase economic activity and environmental impact. Examples also include negative impacts on communities, such as job loss when a technology changes and economic activities move.

records.title: Explain how culture and experience influence people’s perceptions of places and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how culture and experience influence people’s perceptions of places and regions.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how an immigrant and a resident might view a community, how a tourist might see a culture differently than someone who was born and lives there, and how international travel might change a person’s perspective.

records.title: Interpret population pyramids from different countries including birth rates,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Interpret population pyramids from different countries including birth rates, death rates, male-female differences, and the causes and consequences of the age structure of the population.

records.title: Generalize about how human and natural factors have influenced how people make a...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Generalize about how human and natural factors have influenced how people make a living and perform other activities in a place.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how physical features, including mountains, rivers, coasts, deserts, and natural resources, as well as human factors such as political boundaries and accessibility, can affect community size and location. Additional examples might include how groups of people with different levels of economic or political power might choose or be restricted to different locations.

records.title: Human Characteristics of Places
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the human characteristics of places.

records.title: PLACES AND REGIONS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the cultural groups and diversities among people who are rooted in particular places and in human constructs called regions. Analyze the physical and human characteristics of places and regions.

records.title: Interpret and compare climographs from different latitudes and locations.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Interpret and compare climographs from different latitudes and locations.

Examples include but are not limited to: how latitude and elevation impact South American ecosystems, how latitude and seasons affect African ecosystems, and how climate change impacts ecosystems.

records.title: Explain the factors that cause different climate types.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain the factors that cause different climate types.

records.title: Physical Processes
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the physical processes that shape the patterns of the Earth’s surface.

records.title: Locate major ecosystems and explain how and why they are similar or different as a...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate major ecosystems and explain how and why they are similar or different as a consequence of latitude, elevation, land-forms, location, and human activity.

Examples may include but are not limited to: deciduous forest versus prairies in the United States, tropical rain forest versus savanna and desert in Africa, and tundra versus coniferous forests in Canada or Russia.

records.title: Ecosystems
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the characteristics and spatial distribution of ecosystems on Earth’s surface.

records.title: PHYSICAL SYSTEMS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the physical processes that shape the Earth’s surface that, along with plants and animals, are the basis for both sustaining and modifying ecosystems. Identify and analyze the patterns and characteristics of the major ecosystems on Earth.

records.title: Define culture and describe examples of cultural change through diffusion,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Define culture and describe examples of cultural change through diffusion, including what has diffused, why and where it has spread, and positive and negative consequences of the change.

Examples may include but are not limited to: describing the spread of businesses such as fast food franchises, sports like karate or soccer, products like athletic shoes, languages like English, or diseases like the Zika virus.

records.title: Compare and contrast the gender roles assigned to men and women in different...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Compare and contrast the gender roles assigned to men and women in different societies.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how different religions and/or nations assign, expect, or require different roles for men and women, such as who can vote, own property, or hold office. Note that gender roles are culturally defined and vary widely. Within a culture, the majority of traditional roles have varying degrees of acceptance and change over time.

records.title: Describe cultures of the region being studied, including the major languages and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe cultures of the region being studied, including the major languages and religions.

records.title: Explain how culture influences the daily lives of people.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how culture influences the daily lives of people.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how people make a living, raise families, educate children and practice their religion in different cultures and communities.

records.title: Cultural Mosaic
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe the characteristics, distribution, and complexity of Earth’s cultural mosaic.

records.title: Identify and describe the advantages, disadvantages, and impacts of different...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Identify and describe the advantages, disadvantages, and impacts of different technologies used to transport people and products, and spread ideas throughout the world.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the advantages and disadvantages of trucks, trains, ships, and planes for transporting people and/or material; the advantages and disadvantages of print, radio, television, the Internet, and social media for moving information.

records.title: Technology Patterns and Networks
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how technology creates patterns and networks that connect people, resources, products, and ideas.

records.title: Explain how people have modified the environment and used technology to make...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how people have modified the environment and used technology to make places more suitable for humans, as well as how modifications sometimes have negative/unintended consequences.

Examples may include but are not limited to: recovering land in the Netherlands, irrigating deserts or clearing forests for agriculture, and using air conditioning in the southern United States. A technology example might be how irrigation technology changed farming in the Great Plains or how the Green Revolution changed farming in Asia.

records.title: Describe patterns of settlement and explain why people settle where they do and...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe patterns of settlement and explain why people settle where they do and how people make their livings.

Examples may include but are not limited to: coastal and river towns in the past and present, the location of mega-cities, and how people make their livings in different locations. Examples also include forced settlement and/or restrictions on resettlement.

records.title: Explain the patterns, causes, and consequences of major human migrations.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain the patterns, causes, and consequences of major human migrations.

Examples may include but are not limited to: refugee migrations, economic migrations, seasonal migration, and migrations from rural to urban.

records.title: Patterns of Human Settlement
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe patterns, processes, and functions of human settlement.

records.title: Identify factors that contribute to cooperation and conflict between and among...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Identify factors that contribute to cooperation and conflict between and among cultural groups (control/use of natural resources, power, wealth, and cultural diversity).

records.title: Evaluate examples of cooperation and conflict within the region under study from...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Evaluate examples of cooperation and conflict within the region under study from different perspectives.

Examples may include but are not limited to: cooperation between the United States and Canada to protect the fresh water of the Great Lakes, cooperation efforts to stop the spread of diseases among populations, or conflict over control of islands in the South China Sea.

records.title: Forces of Cooperation and Conflict
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain how forces of cooperation and conflict among people influence the division of the Earth’s surface and its resources.

records.title: HUMAN SYSTEMS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain that human activities may be seen on Earth’s surface. Human systems include the way people divide the land, decide where to live, develop communities that are part of the larger cultural mosaic, and engage in the cultural diffusion of ideas and products within and among groups.

records.title: Describe examples of how humans have impacted and are continuing to impact the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe examples of how humans have impacted and are continuing to impact the environment in different places as a consequence of population size, resource use, level of consumption, and technology.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how population pressure impacts deforestation in Brazil, how higher standards of living increase pollution in China, how the use of plastics in the United States can impact water resources, and how use of fossil fuels leads to climate change.

records.title: Explain how different technologies can have positive and negative impacts on the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how different technologies can have positive and negative impacts on the environment.

Examples may include but are not limited to: water management, energy examples include advantages and disadvantages of wind and solar power generation, as well as fracking and tar sands mining; transportation examples might include road and rail transportation and expansion of cities; agricultural examples might include terracing, deforestation, or the use of pesticides and herbicides.

records.title: Analyze ways in which human-induced changes in the physical environment in one...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Analyze ways in which human-induced changes in the physical environment in one place can cause changes in other places.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how cutting forests in one region may result in flooding downstream, how plastic litter in the watershed leads to lake and ocean pollution, how over-fertilization and phosphate use can lead to changes in water quality, and how different factors lead to global climate change, which may impact regions differently.

records.title: Define natural resources and explain how people in different places use, define,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Define natural resources and explain how people in different places use, define, and acquire resources in different ways.

records.title: Humans and the Environment
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how humans use and modify the environment.

records.title: Analyze the effects that a change in the physical environment could have on human...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Analyze the effects that a change in the physical environment could have on human activities and the actions people would be required to make (or would choose to make) in response to the change.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how drought in Africa and Syria is leading to emigration, how coral bleaching is leading to reduced tourism in Australia and the Caribbean, how earthquakes are leading to revised building codes, or how sea level rise is leading to coastal flooding and barrier construction.

records.title: Analyze how combinations of human decisions and natural forces can lead to (or...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Analyze how combinations of human decisions and natural forces can lead to (or help people avoid) a natural disaster.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how building in flood plains increases the likelihood of a natural disaster, and how the federal Soil Conservation Service works to prevent a natural disaster, such as the Dust Bowl.

records.title: Physical and Human Systems
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how physical and human systems shape patterns on the Earth’s surface.

records.title: ENVIRONMENT AND SOCIETY
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain that the physical environment is modified by human activities, which are influenced by the ways in which human societies value and use the Earth’s natural resources, and by Earth’s physical features and processes. Explain how human action modifies the physical environment and how physical systems affect human systems.

records.title: Identify global issues.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Identify global issues.

Examples may include but are not limited to: natural disasters, immigration, food production, food distribution, the impact of climate change, population growth, resource use and depletion, meeting the needs of refugees, migration, poverty, economic development, conflict, and terrorism.

records.title: Investigate a contemporary global issue by applying the skills of geographic inquiry.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Investigate a contemporary global issue by applying the skills of geographic inquiry.

Examples may include but are not limited to: asking geographic questions; acquiring, organizing, and analyzing geographic information; answering geographic questions when practical; using inquiry methods to acquire content knowledge and appropriate data about the issue; identifying the causes and consequences and analyzing the impact, both positive and negative.

records.title: Develop a plan for action:
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Develop a plan for action:

- share and discuss findings of research and issue analysis in group discussions and debates.

- compose a persuasive essay justifying a position with a reasoned argument.

- develop an action plan to address or inform others about the issue, at local to global scales.

records.title: GLOBAL ISSUES
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: A global issue is one that has an impact affecting many regions of the world.

records.subject: social-studies

records.title: Integrate Michigan process and skills standards into a grade-appropriate project....
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Integrate Michigan process and skills standards into a grade-appropriate project. Clearly state a global issue as a question of public policy, trace the origins of the issue, analyze various perspectives, and generate and evaluate alternative resolutions. Identify public policy issues related to global topics and issues studied. For example:

- use Michigan social studies process and skills methods to acquire content knowledge and appropriate data about the issue.

- identify the causes and consequences and analyze the impact, both positive and negative.

- share and discuss findings of research and issue analysis in group discussions and debates.

- compose a persuasive essay justifying a position with a reasoned argument.

- develop an action plan to address or inform others about the issue at a local, national, or global scale.

records.title: Use a variety of geographical tools (maps, globes, geographic information systems...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use a variety of geographical tools (maps, globes, geographic information systems [GIS], and web-based geography technology) to analyze what is happening at different times in different locations.

Examples may include but are not limited to: using maps to explain the Bantu migration patterns and describe their contributions to agriculture, technology, and language environments, or investigating how goods and services flowed in the Roman Empire.

records.title: Apply the skills of geographic inquiry (asking geographic questions, acquiring...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Apply the skills of geographic inquiry (asking geographic questions, acquiring geographic information, organizing geographic information, analyzing geographic information, and answering geographic questions) to analyze a geographic problem or issue.

Examples may include but are not limited to: analyzing the natural and human factors that limited the extent of the Roman Empire.

records.title: Use, interpret, and create maps and graphs representing places and regions in the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use, interpret, and create maps and graphs representing places and regions in the era being studied.

Examples include but are not limited to: using and interpreting maps in historical atlases, creating hand-drawn maps, and using basic GIS.

records.title: Locate and use information from maps and GIS to answer geographic questions on the...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Locate and use information from maps and GIS to answer geographic questions on the era and region being studied.

Examples may include but are not limited to: Google Earth and ArcGIS on-line have multiple teacher applications. Clickable PDFs provide overlay strategies for students without technology skills.

records.title: Geographical Inquiry and Analysis
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Use geographical inquiry and analysis to answer questions about relationships between peoples, cultures, and their environments, and interaction among places and cultures within the era under study.

records.title: THE WORLD IN SPATIAL TERMS
records.subject: social-studies

records.title: Investigations Designed for World History Eras 1-3
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Investigations Designed for World History Eras 1-3 – conduct research on topics and issues, compose persuasive essays, and develop a plan for action.

Era 1 Examples may include but are not limited to: population growth and resources (investigate how population growth affects resource availability) and migration (the significance of migrations of peoples and the resulting benefits and challenges).

Era 2 Examples may include but are not limited to: agriculture (investigate the development of different forms of early or contemporary agriculture and its role in helping societies produce enough food for people, and the consequences of agriculture.

Era 3 Examples may include but are not limited to: trade (investigate the impact of trade and trade routes on civilizations) or power (analyze common factors that influence the rise and fall of empires).

records.title: INVESTIGATION AND ANALYSIS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Throughout the school year, the students are introduced to topics that address issues that integrate time and place. Included are capstone projects that entail the investigation of historical issues that have significance for the student and are clearly linked to the world outside the classroom. The topics and issues are developed as possible capstone projects within units and at the end of the course.

records.title: Identify and describe the advantages, disadvantages, and impacts of different...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Identify and describe the advantages, disadvantages, and impacts of different technologies used to transport products and ideas in the era being studied.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the development of the wheel; different sail, boat, and navigation technologies; road-building technologies in the Incan and Roman Empires; the use of horses in different cultures.

records.title: Technology Patterns and Networks
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how technology creates patterns and networks that connect people, products, and ideas.

records.title: Explain how people in the past have modified the environment and used technology...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how people in the past have modified the environment and used technology to make places more suitable for humans.

Examples may include but are not limited to: agricultural technologies including irrigation.

records.title: Describe patterns of settlement and explain why people settled where they did.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe patterns of settlement and explain why people settled where they did.

Examples may include but are not limited to: areas appropriate for hunter-gatherers or farmers, coastal and/or river towns located for trade, or mountain towns for defense.

records.title: Explain the patterns, causes, and consequences of major human migrations.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain the patterns, causes, and consequences of major human migrations.

Examples may include but are not limited to: early human migration around the world, seasonal migration of pastoral people, and forced migration as a result of war or environmental problems.

records.title: Patterns of Human Settlement
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe patterns, processes, and functions of human settlement.

records.title: Identify factors that contribute to conflict and cooperation between and among...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Identify factors that contribute to conflict and cooperation between and among cultural groups.

Examples may include but are not limited to: conflict over natural resources, trade routes, or wealth.

records.title: Describe examples of cooperation and conflict in the era being studied.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe examples of cooperation and conflict in the era being studied.

Examples may include but are not limited to: conflict among Greek states and the Persian Empire or the expansion of the Roman Empire and the later invasions into the Roman Empire; examples of cooperation through trade/peaceful co-existence include the development of early exchange routes between Europe and Asia and Africa.

records.title: Forces of Cooperation and Conflict
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain how forces of conflict and cooperation among people influence the division of the Earth’s surface and its resources.

records.title: HUMAN SYSTEMS
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: In each era, the language and perspective of geography can help students understand the past and make comparisons with the present.

records.title: Describe examples of how humans modified the environment in the era being studied.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe examples of how humans modified the environment in the era being studied.

Examples may include but are not limited to: how hunter-gatherers, farmers, and pastoral nomads may have used and adapted to different environments in different ways.

records.title: Explain how different technologies were used in the era being studied.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Explain how different technologies were used in the era being studied.

Examples may include but are not limited to: irrigation in major river valley civilizations, island creation among the Aztecs, iron technology in Africa, silk and pottery technology in China.

records.title: Explain how people defined and used natural resources in the era being studied.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain how people defined and used natural resources in the era being studied.

records.title: ENVIRONMENT AND SOCIETY
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Explain how humans used, adapted to, and modified the environment in the era studied.

records.title: WHG ERA 2 – EARLY CIVILIZATIONS AND CULTURES AND THE EMERGENCE OF PASTORAL PEOPLES, 4000 TO 1000 BCE AND WESTERN HEMISPHERE 4000 BCE to 1500 CE
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe and compare defining characteristics of early civilization and pastoral societies, where they emerged, and how they spread. This era includes civilizations in AfroEurasia from 4000 to 1000 BCE as well as cultures in developing the Western Hemisphere from 4000 BCE into Eras 3 and 4 so teachers can compare early civilizations around the globe.

records.title: Grouping for W2
records.subject: social-studies

records.title: Early Civilizations and Major Empires
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze early civilizations and pastoral societies.

records.title: Describe the importance of the development of human communication (oral, visual,...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the importance of the development of human communication (oral, visual, and written) and its relationship to the development of culture.

Examples may include but are not limited to: standardization of physical (rock, bird) and abstract (love, fear) words. In addition, examples may include forms of non-verbal communication from pictographs to abstract writing (governmental administration, laws, codes, history, and artistic expressions).

records.title: Describe how the invention of agriculture led to the emergence of agrarian...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Describe how the invention of agriculture led to the emergence of agrarian civilizations (seasonal harvests, specialized crops, cultivation, and development of villages and towns).

records.title: Use historical and modern maps and other sources to locate, describe, and analyze...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Use historical and modern maps and other sources to locate, describe, and analyze major river systems and discuss the ways these physical settings supported permanent settlements and development of early civilizations.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the Tigris and Euphrates, Huang He, Nile, Indus, and Mississippi rivers.

records.title: Examine early civilizations to describe their common features, including...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Examine early civilizations to describe their common features, including environment, economies, and social institutions.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the Nile, Tigris/Euphrates, and Indus river civilizations in deserts, and Huang He and Mississippi river valley civilizations, and Mesoamerican and Andean civilizations. Topics might include ways of governing, stable food supplies, economic and social structures, use of resources and technology, division of labor, and forms of communication.

records.title: Define the concept of cultural diffusion and explain how ideas and technology...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Define the concept of cultural diffusion and explain how ideas and technology spread from one region to another.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the spread of iron; agriculture; and cultural changes associated with permanent settlements. Cultural diffusion involves identifying the innovation, how it is being spread, who the adopters are, and the intended or unintended consequences of the innovation.

records.title: Describe pastoralism and explain how the climate and geography of Central Asia...
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe pastoralism and explain how the climate and geography of Central Asia were linked to the rise of pastoral societies on the steppes.

Examples may include but are not limited to: the steppes of Central Asia, the savannas of East Africa, the tundra of northern Eurasia, or the mountains of Tibet or South America.

records.title: WHG ERA 3 – CLASSICAL TRADITIONS, WORLD RELIGIONS, AND MAJOR EMPIRES, 1000 BCE TO 300 CE
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze classical civilizations and empires and the emergence of major world religions and large-scale empires. During this era, innovations and social, political, and economic changes occurred through the emergence of classical civilizations in Africa, Eurasia, and the Americas. Africa and Eurasia moved in the direction of human interchange as a result of trade, empire building, and the diffusion of skills and ideas. Similar interactions occurred in the Americas. Six of the world’s major faiths and ethical systems emerged and classical civilizations established institutions, systems of thought, and cultural styles that would influence neighboring peoples and endure for centuries.

records.title: Classical Traditions
records.subject: social-studies
records.text: Analyze classical civilizations and empires and their lasting impact.

records.title: Describe the characteristics that classical civilizations share.
records.subject: social-studies
records.text:
Describe the characteristics that classical civilizations share.

Examples may include but are not limited to: institutions, cultural styles, laws, religious beliefs and practices, and systems of thought that influenced neighboring peoples and have endured for several centuries.

records.title: Create a timeline that illustrates the rise and fall of classical empires during...

records.text: Create a timeline that illustrates the rise and fall of classical empires during the classical period.

records.title: Explain the role of economics in shaping the development of classical...

Explain the role of economics in shaping the development of classical civilizations and empires.

Examples may include but are not limited to: trade routes and their significance, and supply and demand for products.
